newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian youth groups break up Timor meeting.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian youth groups break up Timor meeting.

text.p: A Malaysian youth group allied to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition stormed into a controversial conference on East Timor on Saturday and broke it up, witnesses said.
About 1,000 members of the Malaysian Action Front began chanting outside the hotel in central Kuala Lumpur where the second Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor (APCET) was getting under way.
Yelling "go back, go back" and singing patriotic songs, about 100 youths then entered the hotel and stormed into the fourth floor conference room, vowing to stay until all the participants had left.
As the youths loudly jeered, Malaysian riot police took 36 foreign participants out of the hotel. They were taken in police vans to an immigration detention centre in the capital.
Among them was Hilton Deakin, the Roman Catholic bishop of Melbourne, Australia.

Conference organiser Sanusi Osman said the meeting was effectively scuttled. "We have not decided whether to go ahead with the meeting. But logically, there's no point to go on when all the foreign participants are no longer here."

Malaysian Action Front Secretary-General Saifudin Nasution said the group comprised youth organisations allied to the three main political parties in Mahathir's coalition -- the United Malays National Organisation, the Malaysian Chinese Association and the Malaysian Indian Congress.
Using a bullhorn, Nasution accused the activists -- who sat quietly on the floor looking glum -- of trying to damage ties between Indonesia and Malaysia.
Scores of riot police deployed outside the building to keep more youths from coming into the hotel.

"It has all the hallmarks of an orchestrated act," Fan Yew Ting, a Malaysian human rights activist who was to have spoke at the conference, said amid the shouting. "What we have here is definitely uncivilised and illegal."
Said conference spokesperson Debbie Stothard: "This is a day of shame for me as a Malaysian.
"They have trespassed on private premises. They have been so violent and yelling at us. They have pushed us around. And they put fear in our vistors," she said.

Conference organisers said about 150 foreign delegates from 20 countries had been expected to attend the three-day meeting ahead of Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in the East Timor capital of Dili.
On Wednesday, immigration authorities refused to allow Renato Constantino of the Philippines into the country to attend the conference. He organised the first APCET in Manila in 1994.
Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said earlier in the week the government would find legal ways to stop the meeting, saying it could harm ties with neighbouring Indonesia.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 and annexed it the following year. The United Nations still recognises Lisbon as the administering authority in the territory, located in the far east of the Indonesian archipelago.
